title: Layer 1: fewer false alarms without missing more pumps
what: Reduce Layer 1's false-alarm rate (0.782 on 400 controls) while keeping recall at or above 0.783 on 295 positives (walk-forward, specs/002).
why: When most normal run-ups also get a VETO, people learn to ignore it, and then it fails on the one that matters.
how: New point-in-time features (float from SEC filings, promotion signals, filing cadence), each tested walk-forward with no lookahead. Every result is reported with sample sizes; a precision gain that costs recall must say so.

title: Point-in-time float and market cap for small caps from SEC filings
what: A function float_as_of(symbol, date) that reads shares outstanding and float from SEC filings (10-K, 10-Q, 20-F, F-1, 424B) known on that date.
why: A tiny float is the strongest red flag in FINRA's guidance, and today it is 'unknown' for most small caps, so it is counted as a red flag for everyone.
how: SEC EDGAR (public, free) with a User-Agent contact; parse the cover page and prospectus figures; a test proves nothing filed after the date is used.

title: Paste-a-message red-flag checker
what: A box on the site where someone pastes a message from an investing group and sees which known tactics it uses (free 'professor', 'we all buy together', screenshots for approval, guaranteed returns, compensation trade).
why: The scam happens in the chat. Meeting people at that moment, with their own words, is the warning most likely to work.
how: Rules built from the story tactic tags and the quiz, running only in the browser. Nothing pasted is sent or stored. Never says a stock is a fraud.

title: 'Recovery' scam detector and warning
what: Flag messages that offer to recover lost money for a fee, a 'tax', a deposit or a 'compensation trade'.
why: The second scam targets people who have just lost money; it often takes what is left.
how: Same in-browser rules engine as the message checker, plus a prominent card on the 'Got pumped?' page.

title: Report helper for SEC TCR and FBI IC3
what: A guided form that turns a victim's notes into a ready-to-paste report with a checklist of the evidence to attach.
why: Many victims don't report because it feels pointless or too hard. Reports are how regulators connect cases.
how: Static page; text is generated in the browser and never sent anywhere; links to sec.gov/tcr and ic3.gov.

title: Prebunking cards for groups still in the trust-building phase
what: Short, shareable 'what happens next in groups like this' cards for WhatsApp and Facebook.
why: Warnings shown before the pitch reduce buying (in an OSC study, from 38.1% to 21.3%); generic warnings don't.
how: Content and design work: one image and one link per card, translated where possible.

title: Translate the site, quiz and help page
what: The site, quiz, assistant answers and victim help in more languages.
why: These groups target communities in their own languages.
how: Comment with the language you can help with; a spec will define the translation file format first.

title: Per-brokerage adapters for saved price payloads
what: Convert another brokerage's historical price export into the payload format the parser reads (README, 'Expected file format').
why: So anyone can rebuild the event sets and check the published accuracy with their own data.
how: One adapter function per source plus a synthetic test file; no real data committed.

title: More than one story reviewer
what: Let several trusted reviewers decrypt and approve stories, with an approval log.
why: One reviewer is a bottleneck and a single point of failure.
how: Per-reviewer public keys in the Worker (encrypt to each), a signed approval record. Spec first; the privacy bar is not lowered.

title: Forward validation of Layer 1 from the live scan log (L2.4)
what: Publish Layer 1's live recall and false-alarm rate from the append-only scan log.
why: A backtest is not proof; live results are.
how: Needs about six months of forward rows (around May 2027); the metrics code exists; this issue tracks the review and publication.
